prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, achieved through the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider

statement.case_for: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson is the one result on this shortlist that sits squarely at the centre of fundamental physics: it completed the Standard Model and confirmed the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking. The 2013 prize honoured the theoretical prediction only, so the observation, which took two decades of detector and analysis work, is still unrecognised. It is independently confirmed by two experiments, and the coupling measurements through Run 2 and Run 3 have only strengthened the case. There is no maturity question here, and no earlier prize overlaps with the experimental discovery itself. Having read my colleagues, I still think this is the discovery the committee should identify first, and then find the people behind it.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and I do not want to hide it. A collaboration of thousands produced the result, the three-person limit forces a representative selection, and Della Negra is as defensible a CMS founder as Virdee. Honouring leaders rather than the many who made the measurement risks looking arbitrary. Against that, B053 offers a cleaner two-person attribution, six top-three placements among eight members, and no serious allocation dispute. If the committee decides the Higgs allocation cannot be made defensibly, B053 is the better prize and I would not resist it.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube first, arguing that the diffuse neutrino flux is secure above 5 sigma and that the new window is timely, with Halzen and Spiering as the core credit, and he also ranks the Higgs experiments third with the same trio I propose.
responses.response: We agree on the Higgs names and on the point that the experimental discovery is unrecognised after 2013. Where I qualify his view is the ordering. The diffuse flux is secure, but he himself notes that the individual source associations sit at 3 to 5 sigma, and the prize citation would have to say what has been discovered. For IceCube that is still a window opening, whereas the Higgs is a closed question. I also doubt that Halzen and Spiering alone is a stable allocation, because Karle's role in the AMANDA-to-IceCube detector path is hard to drop. I keep B009 as an alternative, not as the lead.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first because Katori and Ye map cleanly onto the discovery, the field is reproduced across several national laboratories, and the redefinition of the second is approaching.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my own preference and I take it seriously. His point that the attribution is separable from the 2005 comb prize and the ion-clock work is persuasive, and it is a sharp contrast to the Higgs, where I cannot say the credit is clean. I differ on weight. The clock is a refinement of an existing measurement capability, whereas the Higgs answers a question the field had been asking for half a century. I would not call his case metrology rather than discovery, but I do think the discovery claim is weaker. That is why I carry B053 as my first alternative and not lower.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a durable organising principle, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the theory-plus-experiment core, and argues that the 2016 prize did not cover this discovery.
responses.response: I accept his criticism of my own opening trio: leaving out Mele while naming Kane was the weakest choice I made, and his core of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is more defensible than mine. I still disagree that the overlap with 2016 is negligible. That prize was awarded for topological phases and phase transitions, and several colleagues, including Olsson and Kroll, read the overlap as a real cost. The unresolved Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang question, together with the split between 2D and 3D, leaves B013 with an allocation problem about as hard as the Higgs one, without the compensating centrality.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as an instrument-driven advance with unambiguous resolution gains, widely used across materials science, with a coherent trio of Rose, Haider and Urban.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed tidy and the impact is broad, and I do not doubt the maturity. My difficulty is the question of what physics has been discovered. The 1986 microscopy prize is a precedent, but I would want the committee to be clear that it is judging a transformative tool and not a finding about nature. She also notes that Krivanek and the STEM-corrector strand are missing, which weakens the cleanness she claims. I would put it below the discovery-led candidates.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, argues that it complements the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits without duplicating it, and openly flags his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I appreciate that he stated his proximity. His argument that cQED is distinct from the 2025 prize has force, but several others, Lindroth and Pearce among them, see a second superconducting-circuit award so soon as a problem, and the absence of Girvin and Devoret from the credited names makes the allocation hard to defend. I would not exclude B001 on timing alone, but I do not see it as ahead of the Higgs or the clock.

uncertainties: Which three of the four credited ATLAS and CMS figures best represent a collaboration-scale discovery, and whether Della Negra should replace Virdee or Jenni.
Whether the committee will accept a leadership-based selection for a collaboration of thousands, or prefer the cleaner B053.
My account of the roles held at the time of the 2012 announcement is from recollection and is not verified from the supplied material.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate. My own work in string theory and cosmology is not part of any shortlisted discovery.
